key_finding: Every parser in this codebase's own production code (`core::language::adl::parse_adl_source`/`lex_adl`/`collect_block`/`parse_assignments`/`parse_relation`/`parse_constraint_check`, `runtime::parse`, `adapter::dependency::cargo::parse_cargo_lock`, `runtime`'s own hand-rolled `donor-corpus.toml` parser added in a prior generation) is a flat, iterative line/loop-based scanner -- none of them contain a single recursive function call. `syn::parse_file` (used exclusively by `adapter::semantic::rust`) remains the ONLY genuinely recursive-descent parser over externally-admitted, adversarially-shapeable input anywhere in this codebase's production surface. The two `serde_json::from_str`/`from_slice` call sites found (`runtime::census::mod.rs` deserializing Atlas's own previously-serialized `CensusReport` in a round-trip test, and `adapter::dependency::cargo_oracle` deserializing local `cargo metadata` subprocess output into `serde_json::Value` in a `#[cfg(test)]`-only, explicitly never-production-reachable independent oracle) are both outside the production trust boundary this concern is about: one deserializes Atlas's own self-generated data, the other is test-only tooling trusting the locally-installed `cargo` binary, not attacker-controlled network input.
method: Grepped the whole workspace (excluding `.atlas/temporary/donors/` and `target/`) for `fn parse`/`Parser`/`serde_json::from_`, found and read every match in `core/src`, `runtime/src`, `adapter/src`. For `core::language::adl`, read `lex_adl`, `collect_block`, and `parse_adl_source` in full: `collect_block` tracks brace nesting with a flat `i32` depth counter incremented/decremented once per LINE via `str::matches('{').count()`, never recursing per brace, per nesting level, or per declaration -- structurally unlike `syn`'s `Expr`/`Item` recursive-descent tree construction. For `adapter::dependency::cargo::parse_cargo_lock`, confirmed the same shape: a `while let Some(line) = lines.next()` loop with one level of nested `while` for a package's own field lines, no recursive function calls. For the two `serde_json` call sites, read their surrounding module doc comments to confirm trust boundary and production-reachability.

design_decisions.question: Is a code-review conclusion ('no recursive function calls found') sufficient evidence, or does the claim need an empirical/adversarial test the way `max_structural_recursion_risk`'s own four vectors were each confirmed by real-process reproduction?
design_decisions.decision: Added one empirical test rather than relying on code review alone, consistent with this session's own established discipline of confirming a claim empirically wherever practical. `core::language::adl::tests::parser_handles_adversarially_deep_brace_nesting_without_recursion_or_crash` feeds `parse_adl_source` 200,000 nested braces (two orders of magnitude past the deepest confirmed `syn` crash vector, 3,000 `if`/`else` arms) on adjacent lines and confirms it parses successfully in well under a second on the default test-thread stack -- proving the absence of recursion-driven stack growth empirically, not merely by reading the loop structure.

design_decisions.question: Should `EXTRACTION_STACK_SIZE`'s large-stack-worker pattern be applied preemptively to the ADL parser or the Cargo.lock parser anyway, as defense-in-depth, even though no recursion exists to protect against?
design_decisions.decision: No. That pattern exists specifically to buy headroom against recursion depth proportional to adversarial input structure; wrapping an already-O(1)-stack iterative loop in a dedicated large-stack worker thread would add real complexity (thread spawn overhead, `AssertUnwindSafe`-shaped code, a second stack-size constant to maintain) for zero actual protection, since there is no stack growth to bound in the first place. Defense-in-depth is valuable against a real, non-zero residual risk (as it was for `syn`, where a 5th undiscovered vector remains possible); it is not valuable applied to a structurally different, already-flat algorithm.

stable_validator_law_compliance.claim: No parser in this codebase's own production code, other than `syn::parse_file` inside `adapter::semantic::rust` (already mitigated by `EXTRACTION_STACK_SIZE`/`max_structural_recursion_risk`), has a recursion-depth-proportional-to-input-structure stack-overflow risk. This is a definitive, evidenced negative result for the open question the prior generation explicitly left unanswered, not a claim that no other security concern of any kind exists in these parsers.
stable_validator_law_compliance.self_written_evidence: The new adversarial test is the falsifiable claim itself: if `core::language::adl`'s parser DID recurse per brace the way `syn` recurses per bracket/operator/keyword, 200,000 nested levels would reproduce the same class of stack-overflow abort this session already confirmed for `syn` at far shallower depths (300-3,000 levels) on a comparable default test-thread stack. It does not -- the test passes in ~0.2s.
